Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Oct 28, 2026

Wednesday ✅.

Today's newsletter is 784 words, a 3-minute read.

📈 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed up 0.3%.

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Oracle (+10.7%) provided anxious investors with a soothing long-term outlook, saying it expects to be cash flow positive by 2028.
 
 
1 big thing: Cloudy with a chance of cash
By Pete Gannon
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios
 

A pair of hyperscalers reported results after today's bell. Investors' initial take: They liked what they saw at Microsoft, and not so much at Google.

💵 Zoom in: Cash flow was an immediate focus.

  • Google's free cash flow, which had turned negative last quarter under the weight of massive AI spending, deteriorated further to negative $9.1 billion in Q3, a bigger drop than Wall Street was expecting.
  • Microsoft's free cash flow also fell, by 27%, but remained positive at $18.6 billion in the September quarter.

💰 Follow the money: Both companies continue to spend massively on AI infrastructure.

  • For Google, capex totaled $51.4 billion in Q3, up 114% from a year earlier.
  • Microsoft spent $39.4 billion in the quarter, a 103% increase from a year ago.

Stunning stat: Together, that's nearly $91 billion in just three months.

⛅️ Cloud growth was a bright spot for both companies.

  • Google Cloud revenue surged 103% year over year to $30.7 billion.
  • Microsoft's Azure cloud revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion.
  • Both exceeded analysts' growth expectations.

🔍 What we're watching: For Google, the strong cloud performance was overshadowed by disappointing results in its core advertising and search business.

  • Google advertising revenue grew 11% to $82 billion, below analysts' expectations.

📉 📈 The impact: Shares of Google parent Alphabet were down over 10% in extended trading, while Microsoft was up around 3%.
 
 
2. A Fed pause, with some discord
 

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh speaking to reporters today. Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

The Fed held interest rates steady today, but the decision was not unanimous.

  • Two officials, Fed governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of a quarter-point hike, Axios' Neil Irwin writes.

🔍 Zoom in: The Fed said it needs more information to determine the appropriate policy stance and described the economy as expanding at a "strong" pace, up from "solid" in September.

  • Traders now see a 79% chance of a December rate hike, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

🤖 The intrigue: Warsh pushed back on the notion that the AI investment boom is insulated from higher interest rates, citing widening credit spreads and signs of investors becoming more selective.

  • "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything," the Fed chairman said. "I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."

🏛️ What we're watching: Cook is the Fed governor President Trump is seeking to fire. It was her first dissent as a Fed official, coming ahead of a White House hearing on her potential removal over alleged mortgage fraud.
 
 
3. Other happenings
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

⚖️ Weil, Gotshal & Manges is planning to wind down its operations, its leaders reportedly told partners today. (FT)

🤝 DoorDash is closing in on a deal to buy Instacart. (CNBC)

📦 FedEx raised its profit and sales guidance for the year, the latest package carrier to signal strength heading into the holiday shopping season. (Bloomberg)

4. A cruise awakening
 

Image courtesy of Villa Vie Residences
 

Villa Vie Residences' continuous world cruise has run out of gas, Pete writes.

Zoom in: The Florida-based company — which offers "permanent residency" in rooms ranging from roughly $120,000 to $440,000, plus thousands more a month in fees — has ordered residents off its 640-foot cruise ship while at port in Cambodia.

  • ⛽️ The reason: It can't afford to refuel.

Catch up quick: The ship, the Villa Vie Odyssey, was two years into a planned three-and-a-half year long "continuous voyage around the world."

  • It suspended operations yesterday as it "works to address extraordinary increases in fuel costs and evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives."

What they're saying: The Odyssey has been operating in South Asia since August, per its itinerary, and the company said fuel costs in the region "have risen sharply."

  • Monthly fuel expenses, measured per equivalent cabin, have more than tripled from historic levels, it says.
  • 🗣️ "Since the [Iran] conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," the company said. "Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."

💭 Pete's thought bubble: Homeownership is expensive enough without having to worry about a quarter-million gallons of fuel.
